title: How big can a slip of the decimal point be?
description: A council meant to send one point eight million euros but sent one hundred eighty eight million, and a medicine dose of zero point zero five milligrams is read as zero point five. Each slip is measured by how many times larger the number became. The close ties it to real life.
teaching_notes: One idea: a slip of the decimal point or of the unit changes a number by ten times or one hundred times. Watch for students who think a small slip in the digits makes a small change in the amount.

source: In 2013 a council meant to send 1.8 million euros but sent 1
video_script.why: The child has learned to read and compare decimals and now sees how a slip with the point or the unit changes an amount.
video_script.substitution: Compare the two amounts with place value, and say how many times larger the slip made the number.
video_script.anchor: A council that sent far more money than it meant to, and a medicine dose with a misplaced decimal point.
video_script.payoff_line: Check the unit and the place of the decimal point

final_answer.value: About 100 times larger; the medicine dose would be 10 times larger
final_answer.spoken: about one hundred times larger; the medicine dose would be ten times larger

hold_back: About 100 times larger; the medicine dose would be 10 times larger
maths_rules: 1 euro-cent = 1/100 euro, so counting in cents makes a number 100 times bigger
0.05 = 5 hundredths, 0.5 = 5 tenths, and 5 tenths = 10 x 5 hundredths
so reading 0.05 mg as 0.5 mg gives a dose 10 times too big
video_script.design: The two amounts of money sit side by side with the digits lined up, then the digit strip for 0.05 and 0.5 shows the five moving one place left. Each slip is labelled with how many times larger it made the number.
